items.text: A political science PhD is not a one-way ticket into a lecture hall.
The confusion for most PhD holders is not a shortage of options.
The order below follows real growth and growth headroom as you gain reputation and proof, not which title sounds most respectable at a family gathering.
Advisory work for companies, campaigns, or institutions, plus a publicly owned research or commentary platform built on your specialisation.
Pay and influence grow with published output and policy access, not tenure alone.

blocks.heading: Independent Research Consulting and a Commentary Platform

items.text: This is the track most PhD holders underuse, because academic training rewards writing for three peer reviewers, not for a paying client or a public audience.

A related and often underrated version: building your own research platform, a policy newsletter, a data-driven explainer series, or a niche consulting practice in your exact sub-field (electoral behaviour, federalism, foreign policy of a specific region, and so on), that you own outright instead of publishing only inside academic journals few outside your field will ever read.

Why this scales when the others don't: you set your own pricing instead of sitting on a UGC or government pay scale, demand repeats with every election cycle, policy debate, or regulatory shift rather than depending on one employer's budget, and once you have a track record you can bring on research assistants instead of doing every hour yourself.

blocks.heading: Senior Think-Tank and Policy Research Roles

items.text: Research associate and policy analyst roles at institutions such as the Observer Research Foundation, Carnegie India, the Centre for Policy Research, the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses, and the Takshashila Institution are usually where a fresh graduate enters this world.
That matters for pay and influence both.
Reliable public pay figures at Senior Fellow or Director level are scarce because most institutions negotiate senior compensation individually rather than publishing a scale.

blocks.heading: How Assistant Professor Hiring Actually Works

items.text: Most PhD holders know they need to clear UGC-NET/JRF and finish the doctorate.
Universities score applications on a points system covering your degrees, publications, teaching experience, and research contributions before shortlisting anyone for the next stage.

A department or university selection committee narrows the screened pool further, often favouring candidates with publications, prior teaching experience, and a subject specialisation that matches an open post's specific requirement.

blocks.heading: Competition That Restarts After Your Viva

items.text: Two tracks on this list share a pattern the "just clear NET and finish the PhD" framing hides completely: clearing the well-known filter does not end the competition.
You qualified UGC-NET/JRF, found a funded or self-financed seat, and spent roughly four to seven years, sometimes longer, finishing original research under a supervisor.

A confirmed assistant professor post typically runs through paper screening against a points-based academic record, a shortlisting round, a selection-committee interview, and increasingly a demonstration lecture in front of the department.

Before you commit further years, an ad-hoc teaching contract, a UPSC attempt, an unpaid international fellowship, or a leap into consulting, run the track you are leaning toward through The four questions .
Academia and senior think-tank research reward people who like long solitary reading and writing, mentoring, and slow-building arguments.
You have already spent years of income and, often, family patience on the doctorate.

blocks.heading: Track Before You Commit Further Years

items.text: A qualification checklist tells you what is formally required.
Do not accept an ad-hoc contract, start UPSC prep, or apply to an international fellowship before passing all three proofs below.

One peer-reviewed or serious working paper beyond your dissertation, one policy brief written to a real institution's format, or one data-backed research note on a live policy question, not just the dissertation abstract restated.
Hiring committees at serious institutions look for publications, briefs, fieldwork, and a specific specialisation beyond the dissertation.
Confirm your exact age-limit and attempt count for your category before committing a year of prep.
Ad-hoc and guest-faculty work has kept many qualified PhDs afloat for years at a stretch across Indian universities, not months.

blocks.heading: Realistic Pay Across All 5 Tracks
rows: Independent research consulting & commentary platform
Highly variable, upside-driven

Income scales with client base, retainers, speaking fees, and book or column income rather than a fixed band. A well-known specialist can out-earn a full professor; a specialist with no visible track record earns very little at first.
Senior think-tank / policy research (Fellow, Senior Fellow)
Meaningfully above fresh-graduate research-associate pay; director-level figures are scarce publicly

A PhD typically enters above the entry research-associate rung that a fresh graduate starts on. Institutions such as the Observer Research Foundation, Carnegie India, the Centre for Policy Research, and the Takshashila Institution set senior pay individually rather than on a public scale.
International bodies & multilateral organisations
UN-system P-scale and equivalent bands, often well above Indian academic or government pay

Entry is commonly through a Junior Professional Officer programme, a fellowship, or years of field/research experience before a P-2 or P-3 post. Verify current post-adjustment figures on the specific agency's official careers page.
UPSC / civil services (IAS, IPS, IFS, State PSC)
₹56,100/month basic at entry (Level 10), rising over roughly 37 years to a single Cabinet Secretary post at ₹2.5 lakh/month
The same fixed central Group A scale applies regardless of a PhD. A doctorate can sharpen your optional-subject and interview depth, but it does not change the pay ladder or the age-limit rules.
Academia: permanent Assistant Professor (post-PhD)
UGC/state scale from Level 10 basic ₹57,700/month once confirmed; ad-hoc and guest-faculty pay is considerably lower and often per lecture
Many recent PhDs spend years on ad-hoc or guest contracts, with no guaranteed income during vacation months, before a permanent post opens, if one opens at all in their specific sub-field and region.

blocks.heading: Why a Phd Changes the Decision

items.text: You have already spent 4-7+ years and cleared UGC-NET/JRF, a fresh graduate is choosing whether to start that; you are choosing what to do with it now that it is done.
Your remaining UPSC attempts and age-limit window are almost certainly smaller than a fresh graduate's, simply because the doctorate took years.
You can enter a think tank at Fellow or Senior Fellow level, not the entry research-associate rung most fresh graduates start at.
Ad-hoc and guest-faculty pay, and the wait for a permanent post, are a real near-term reality specific to people who have already finished a PhD, not a hypothetical future problem.

blocks.heading: AI Is Doing to Political Science Research

items.text: First-pass literature reviews and summarising long documents, judgments, or committee reports are already shifting into AI-assisted workflows at many think tanks and research teams.

Routine data cleaning and basic descriptive analysis of survey or voting datasets is now faster with AI tools than doing it by hand, which reduces demand for pure data-entry-adjacent research support roles.

Generic explainer writing on well-covered topics is easier to automate than original fieldwork or a genuinely new argument, so purely summarising commentary carries more exposure than original analysis.

blocks.heading: Skills That Matter After a Phd

items.text: Translation writing , turning a dissertation chapter or a journal argument into a policy brief, an op-ed, or a client memo that a non-specialist can actually use.
Data literacy , comfort with survey data, government datasets, and basic quantitative methods, even for a primarily qualitative researcher.
Public speaking and media handling , explaining your specialisation clearly on a panel, in an interview, or in a classroom.
Negotiation and stakeholder management , the human layer behind consulting, international-body work, and civil services that AI does not touch.
A working foreign language relevant to your specialisation , a genuine differentiator for international-body and multilateral-organisation roles specifically, less critical for the domestic tracks.
Practical AI fluency , using AI tools to speed up literature review and drafting while personally verifying every output, per the AI section above.
